description: We are two Bay Area students who are super passionate about Space Technology and Remote Sensing. Our skillsets are combination of 3D Modeling, CAD, Data Analysis, Remote Sensing, and Data Visualization, and our goal is to tackle environmental problems that haven't already been fixed.
summary:
Helios tackles the MODIS-VIIRS harmonization challenge by bringing both sensors fire records into one site, giving users a complete view of fire activity from 2000 to today. Built on Google Earth Engine, it lets users switch between NASA MODIS and VIIRS hotspot data while using the same daily burning-activity calendar and area readouts on a spinning 3D globe: red for MODIS, yellow for VIIRS, orange where both see fire.

Because we believe fire, air, and land are all interconnected, Helios pairs hotspots with Sentinel-5P SO₂ values and Sentinel-2 burn scars, letting users analyze smoke levels and air quality index. Helios raises watch levels when fire and pollution spike, and lets you save places. In the US, it puts official agency wildfire reports next to what the satellites saw.

To help users understand why the two sensors see fire differently, we built CAD models of NOAA-20 VIIRS and NASA Terra MODIS that show how each satellite works. Watch animated satellite passes sweep across your area, as well as a 3D wildfire render grows with the fire’s size and lets you hover over the fire, heat, smoke, burn scar and air quality.

To fully analyze the data, Helios has a daily burning-activity calendar and a 25-year history showing seasonal patterns and whether this month is busier than usual as well as a time-lapse of a year of fires in 26 secs.

Overall, our mission was to create a tool that helps people who live in wildfire-prone areas (like us) understand the fires around them.
details:
We grew up in California watching our parents call relatives and flip through news channels just to learn where a fire was and whether we were safe. So we built Helios, a web application (which is live) that turns satellite data into one fire map anyone can read.

Helios doesn't only detect fires. It combines four satellite datasets from two space agencies to show the whole background of the fire:

  • NASA MODIS (Terra and Aqua, since 2000), through NASA FIRMS: the long-term fire record, going back 25 years.
  • NASA VIIRS VNP14A1 (since 2012): sharper fire detections that catch smaller fires MODIS misses.
  • ESA Sentinel-5P: sulfur dioxide in the air, which shows how smoke and pollution spread beyond the flames.
  • ESA Sentinel-2: burn scars and burn severity (dNBR), which show what the fire left behind.

Because MODIS and VIIRS see the ground at different resolutions, their fire counts can’t be compared directly. Helios harmonizes them by scaling MODIS to match VIIRS, turning 2000 to today into one fire record (which is a feature the user could choose, or they can stick to choosing a singular instrument.)

We also built features that make the data easy to understand, even if you’ve never heard of MODIS or VIIRS:

  • Layer toggles: turn active fires, sulfur dioxide and burn scars on or off for the chosen Area of Interest
  • 3D fire render: an illustrated fire paired with real satellite numbers made with Blender.
  • Time-lapse: press play to watch fires spread day by day.
  • Watch a pass: an animation of how each satellite sweeps over your area.
  • Local snapshot: fire pixels, burned area and sulfur dioxide, compared to the 30-day normal.
  • Burn calendar: every month since 2000 as a fire heat map, with seasonal patterns and yearly trends.
  • Fire history in context: plain-language comparisons like “busier than 100% of past Junes.
  • Export: download hotspot records, monthly summaries and calendar images for reports.

We use Google Earth Engine to pull and process all four satellite datasets (FIRMS, Sentinel)

We designed the 3D satellite models using Blender & Meshy: MODIS on the Terra satellite and VIIRS on NOAA-20.

Our Python backend, served with Uvicorn and hosted on Render, harmonizes MODIS with VIIRS.

The frontend is built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript.

  • MapLibre GL JS draws the interactive fire map on a CARTO basemap built from OpenStreetMap data.
  • Nominatim powers place search.
  • Three.js renders the 3D fire and the satellite models.
